html:
The big picture

Kinematics described how bodies move; dynamics explains why: forces. Newton's axioms are the rules. (1) The principle of inertia: without a net force a body keeps its velocity. (2) The action principle \vec F = m\vec a: a net force gives the body an acceleration in its direction, more generally \vec F = \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt with the momentum \vec p = m\vec v. With several forces their vector sum counts, \sum_i \vec F_i = m\vec a, counting only forces acting on the body. (3) The reaction principle: forces come in pairs of equal size and opposite direction, acting on the two different bodies. Two forces appear everywhere: the gravitational force \vec F_g = m\vec g and the normal force F_N with which a surface pushes back. All examples follow one recipe: pick one body, collect the forces on it, set \sum_i \vec F_i = m\vec a (or = \vec 0 if it is static), split into components, solve: a car, a person in an elevator, a street light on two ropes, a pulley block, two strings on one mass.

1 Force

Lecture: p. 2 · Giancoli §4-1

Dynamics asks why bodies move as they do. The answer is forces: a push or a pull exerted on a body by something else (a hand, a rope, the ground, the Earth's gravity). A force has a size and a direction, so it is a vector and adds like one (2 Vectors and Vector Products). Its unit, the newton, follows from axiom 2 (section 3). Newton's three axioms (board: "Newton Axioms") say how forces and motion are related.

2 Axiom 1: the principle of inertia

Lecture: p. 2 · Giancoli §4-2

The board only names it: 1. Principle of inertia. Its content: a body on which no net force acts keeps its velocity, both size and direction. At rest it stays at rest; in motion it moves on in a straight line at constant speed. Forces are not needed to keep things moving, only to change their motion. (It also follows from axiom 2: \vec F = \vec 0 \Rightarrow \vec a = \vec 0 \Rightarrow \vec v constant.)

The law holds as stated only for an observer who is not accelerating himself (an inertial reference frame, e.g. the ground for everyday purposes). In an accelerating car, a cup starts sliding without any force pushing it; that "push" is a pseudo effect of the accelerating frame, like the centrifugal acceleration in 7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion.

Common mistake — "a moving body needs a force to keep going"

A ball rolling on the floor slows down, so it's tempting to think motion "uses up" a force. The ball slows because friction and air resistance act against its motion: a net force backwards gives a backwards acceleration. Without them it wouldn't slow down. A force along the motion is only needed to cancel those resistances, e.g. a car at constant 100 km/h whose engine force equals drag plus rolling friction (9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction).

3 Mass and axiom 2: the action principle

Lecture: p. 2 · Giancoli §4-3, §4-4

2. Action principle (board):

\vec F = m\,\vec a = m\cdot\ddot{\vec r}, \qquad \vec a = \frac{\vec F}{m}

[F] = \mathrm{kg\,m/s^2} = \mathrm N, [m] = \mathrm{kg}, [a] = \mathrm{m/s^2}.

Symbols
  • \vec F — the (net) force on the body (N, newton = \mathrm{kg\,m/s^2})
  • m — the body's mass (kg)
  • \vec a — its acceleration (m/s²); \ddot{\vec r} — second time derivative of its position, the same thing (4 Kinematics – Position, Velocity and Acceleration)

[F] = [m]\,[a] = \mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{m/s^2}, and that combination gets its own name: one newton is the force that accelerates 1\,\mathrm{kg} at 1\,\mathrm{m/s^2} (a 100\,\mathrm g apple weighs about 1\,\mathrm N). The second form, \vec a = \vec F/m, reads the law the other way: the force is the cause, the acceleration the effect, and the same force accelerates a heavy body less. Mass here measures inertia: how hard it is to change a body's velocity. Since m > 0, \vec a always points the same way as \vec F.

Several forces (board, "Multiple forces"):

\sum_i \vec F_i = m\cdot\vec a

↳ all forces acting on the body.

Symbols
  • \vec F_i — the i-th force acting on the body (N); \sum_i — their vector sum, the net force
  • m, \vec a — mass and acceleration of that one body

Forces add like vectors, and only the sum shows up in the acceleration. A book on a table feels gravity and the table's push, two non-zero forces, but their sum is \vec 0 and it doesn't accelerate. In practice the sum is written in components, one equation per axis: \sum F_x = m\,a_x, \sum F_y = m\,a_y. "All forces acting on the body" is the important phrase: forces the body exerts on other things don't belong in its sum.

Example: force on a car

"Estimate force needed to accelerate a car with m = 1000\ \mathrm{kg} at 0.5\,g."

F = m\cdot a = 1000\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot 0.5\cdot 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2} = 4.9\ \mathrm{kN}
Symbols
  • F — size of the net force on the car (N); m — mass of the car (kg); a = 0.5\,g — its acceleration (m/s²)

"At 0.5\,g" means half the free-fall acceleration, 4.905\,\mathrm{m/s^2}; so F = 4905\,\mathrm N \approx 4.9\,\mathrm{kN}. "Estimate" because this is the net force; the engine must also overcome drag and rolling friction.

"Force needed to stop the car from v_0 = 100\ \mathrm{km/h} in a distance s = 55\ \mathrm m."

v_0 = \frac{100\ \mathrm{km/h}}{3.6\ \frac{\mathrm{km/h}}{\mathrm{m/s}}} = 27.8\ \mathrm{m/s}
Symbols
  • v_0 — speed before braking (m/s); s — braking distance (m)

1\,\mathrm{km/h} = \frac{1000\,\mathrm m}{3600\,\mathrm s} = \frac{1}{3.6}\,\mathrm{m/s}, which is what "3.6\,\frac{\mathrm{km/h}}{\mathrm{m/s}}" says. Next the board writes "v = \sqrt{2as}, start from v_0 = 0": the time-free law of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall, used because a distance and no time is given. Written out for braking:

\begin{aligned} 0 &= v_0^2 + 2a\,s && \text{(time-free law; the car stops, } v_1 = 0) \\ a &= -\frac{v_0^2}{2s} = -\frac{(27.8\ \mathrm{m/s})^2}{2\cdot 55\ \mathrm m} \approx -7\ \mathrm{m/s^2} && \text{(solve for } a\text{, insert)} \\ F &= m\cdot a \approx -7000\ \mathrm N && \text{(axiom 2, same } 1000\,\mathrm{kg} \text{ car)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • a — the constant braking acceleration (m/s²), negative = against the motion
  • F — braking force (N); the minus sign means it points backwards

"Start from v_0 = 0" reads it backwards: braking from 27.8\,\mathrm{m/s} to 0 in 55 m mirrors accelerating from 0 to 27.8\,\mathrm{m/s} in 55 m, with the same \lvert a\rvert. The board's middle step drops the minus sign; the result -7\,\mathrm{m/s^2} has it. Size check: 7\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \approx 0.7\,g, a typical full braking on a dry road, which has to come from the tyres' friction (9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction).

4 Momentum: the general form of axiom 2

Lecture: p. 2 · Giancoli §9-1

The action principle in section 3 links force to acceleration. Newton himself wrote it with a different quantity, which the lecture introduces next: the momentum, mass times velocity.

\vec p = m\cdot\vec v \qquad (\text{Impuls})
Symbols
  • \vec p — momentum of the body (kg·m/s), mass times velocity (German Impuls)
  • m — mass (kg); \vec v — velocity (m/s)

Momentum is a vector pointing along \vec v; it measures "how much motion" a body carries. A slow truck and a fast tennis ball can have the same momentum. To change a body's momentum, a force is needed, and the faster you want to change it, the larger the force. That is the action principle in its original, more general form:

\vec F = \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(m\cdot\vec v) \qquad [\text{more general}]
Symbols
  • \vec F — net force on the body (N)
  • \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} — rate at which the momentum changes (kg·m/s² = N)

In words: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. For a constant mass it turns back into the familiar form (board: "if m = constant"):

\vec F = \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(m\cdot\vec v) = m\,\frac{\mathrm d\vec v}{\mathrm dt} = m\cdot\vec a

Symbols as above; \vec a = \mathrm d\vec v/\mathrm dt — acceleration (m/s²). The constant m comes out of the derivative, and the derivative of the velocity is the acceleration.

Why "more general": differentiate the product m\vec v with the product rule,

\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(m\,\vec v) = \dot m\,\vec v + m\,\dot{\vec v} = \dot m\,\vec v + m\,\vec a
Symbols
  • \dot m — rate of change of the mass (kg/s); other symbols as above

With constant mass, \dot m = 0 and only m\vec a is left (the board's last line). The momentum form also covers situations where no single body with a fixed mass accelerates, such as a stream of material being stopped or a conveyor belt being loaded; there the force goes into changing the momentum of the material that arrives. (Bodies that lose or gain mass, like rockets, need careful bookkeeping of what belongs to the system; Giancoli treats this in §9-10.) \vec F = m\vec a is the special case.

Worked example — force of a water jet on a wall

A cleaning robot sprays 0.5\ \mathrm{kg} of water per second horizontally at 20\ \mathrm{m/s} against a wall; the water stops there and runs down.

  1. Momentum arriving per second: each second, 0.5\ \mathrm{kg} with 20\ \mathrm{m/s} loses the momentum 0.5\cdot20 = 10\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}.
  2. Force on the water: F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{10\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}}{1\ \mathrm s} = 10\ \mathrm N, against the jet.
  3. Force on the wall: by the reaction principle (section 5), 10\ \mathrm N into the wall. Check of units: \mathrm{kg/s}\cdot\mathrm{m/s} = \mathrm{kg\,m/s^2} = \mathrm N ✓.
  4. Point: no single body with a constant mass accelerates here, yet \vec F = \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt gives the force directly.
Connection

Momentum comes back in 12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions: in a collision the forces are unknown, but the total momentum of the colliding bodies is conserved.

5 Axiom 3: the reaction principle

Lecture: p. 3 · Giancoli §4-5

"If a force acting on a body has its origin in another body, then a force of the same magnitude but opposite direction will act on the second body."

Push on a desk and the desk pushes back on your hand, equally hard and in the opposite direction. The two forces act on different bodies: one on the desk, one on the hand. (Giancoli Fig. 4-8)

Textbook figure: an assistant pulls a sled with a block of marble. Force pairs: on the sled exerted by the assistant \vec F_\text{SA} = -\vec F_\text{AS} (force on the assistant exerted by the sled); friction force on the sled exerted by the ground \vec F_\text{SG} and force on the ground exerted by the sled \vec F_\text{GS} = -\vec F_\text{SG}; force on the ground exerted by the assistant \vec F_\text{GA} = -\vec F_\text{AG} (force on the assistant exerted by the ground). Added on the board: \vec F_g on the assistant (blue, down).

The labels: \vec F_\text{SA} = force on S(led) by A(ssistant), first letter who feels it, second who exerts it. Each pair swaps the letters and flips the sign. The two forces of a pair never cancel each other, because they act on different bodies, and whether a body accelerates depends only on the forces on it. The assistant moves forward because the ground pushes her forward (\vec F_\text{AG}) harder than the sled pulls her back (\vec F_\text{AS}); the sled moves because she pulls it harder than the ground's friction holds it back.

Question (board): a truck collides with a passenger car. Which vehicle experiences the larger force? Neither: by the reaction principle the force of the truck on the car and the force of the car on the truck are equal in size and opposite. What differs is the effect: by a = F/m the same force gives the light car a much larger acceleration (10 t truck, 1 t car: ten times larger), which is why the car and its passengers are hurt more.

Common mistake — "the truck pushes harder"

The heavier or faster body does not exert the larger force on the other. Equal forces, unequal accelerations.

6 Weight and the normal force

Lecture: p. 3–4 · Giancoli §4-6

Gravitational force (board):

\vec F_g = m\,\vec g

↳ points towards the centre of the Earth. "This force acts on every body on the surface of the Earth, also stationary objects."

Symbols
  • \vec F_g — the gravitational force (the body's weight) (N)
  • m — mass of the body (kg); \vec g — gravitational acceleration, g \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, pointing to the Earth's centre (down)

In free fall the only force is the weight and the acceleration is \vec g, so axiom 2 gives \vec F_g = m\vec g. The weight doesn't switch off when a body rests on a table; it is still there, balanced by another force:

Textbook figure: a bust standing on a table. On the bust: \vec F_G (down) and \vec F_N (up); on the table: \vec F'_N (down).

  • F_N is the force that the table exerts on the object.
  • F'_N is the force that the object exerts on the table.

A table is not perfectly rigid: the bust compresses it very slightly, and the table pushes back, perpendicular ("normal") to its surface. This normal force \vec F_N grows exactly as large as needed to stop the bust sinking in. For the bust at rest, \vec F_N + \vec F_G = \vec 0, so here F_N = mg, but only because nothing accelerates (the elevator below is the counter-example). \vec F_N and \vec F'_N are a reaction pair: table on bust, bust on table.

The normal force is not always equal to the weight; it adjusts to whatever keeps the box from moving into or off the table. Left: nothing else acts, F_N = mg. Middle: a hand pushes down with 40 N, F_N = mg + 40\,\mathrm N. Right: a rope pulls up with 40 N, F_N = mg - 40\,\mathrm N. (Giancoli Fig. 4-15)

Common mistake — weight and normal force as a reaction pair

On the bust, \vec F_G and \vec F_N are equal and opposite, so it's tempting to call them an action–reaction pair. They aren't: both act on the same body, and they're equal only because the bust doesn't accelerate. The partner of \vec F_N is \vec F'_N; the partner of \vec F_G (Earth on bust) is the bust's pull on the Earth.

Example: person in an elevator

Textbook figure: a person standing on a scale in an elevator; the acceleration \vec a (orange), the weight m\vec g and the normal force \vec F_N (magenta).

Person in elevator, m = 65\ \mathrm{kg}. The elevator accelerates with a = 0.2\,g. Which force is exerted on the human during this acceleration? The elevator reaches a velocity of 2\ \mathrm{m/s} and stops accelerating. Which force is acting now?

The body is the person. The forces on it: the weight mg (down) and the normal force F_N from the floor (up); nothing else touches the person. The board's equation counts down as positive (the weight enters with +, the upward F_N with -), with a the size of a downward acceleration. "Forces acting on the body, \sum \vec F_i = m\vec a":

mg - F_N = m\cdot a \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_N = mg - ma = m\cdot g - 0.2\,g\cdot m = 0.8\,g\cdot m \approx 510\ \mathrm N
Symbols
  • mg — the person's weight (N), down
  • F_N — the normal force from the floor (scale) on the person (N), up: what the scale measures
  • a = 0.2\,g \approx 1.96\,\mathrm{m/s^2} — the elevator's (and person's) acceleration

F_N = 0.8 \cdot 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \cdot 65\,\mathrm{kg} \approx 510\,\mathrm N instead of the usual 638\,\mathrm N: the person "feels lighter", and the scale shows 510/9.81 \approx 52\,\mathrm{kg}.

With v = 2\ \mathrm{m/s} and a = 0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}:

m\cdot g - F_N = m\cdot a = 0\ \mathrm N, \qquad F_N = m\cdot g = 637\ \mathrm N \quad (g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2})

Symbols as above. Constant velocity means zero acceleration (axiom 1), so the floor carries exactly the weight, 65 \cdot 9.81 = 637.65\,\mathrm N. The point of the second question: only the acceleration matters, not the velocity. Moving at 2\,\mathrm{m/s} or standing still, the scale shows the same.

Unclear (p. 4): direction of the acceleration

The board doesn't say whether the elevator accelerates up or down. The equation mg - F_N = ma is for a downward acceleration (starting to go down, or braking while going up). For an upward acceleration of 0.2\,g the same method gives F_N = 1.2\,mg \approx 765\,\mathrm N. The figure's arrow doesn't settle it either.

Worked example — accelerating upwards

An 80 kg robot technician stands on a scale in an elevator that starts upwards with a = 0.1\,g.

  1. Choose an axis: up positive.
  2. Forces on the person: +F_N (floor, up) and -mg (weight, down).
  3. Axiom 2: F_N - mg = ma, so F_N = m(g + a) = 80 \cdot 1.1 \cdot 9.81 \approx 863\,\mathrm N.
  4. Interpret: the scale shows 863/9.81 \approx 88\,\mathrm{kg}; the person "feels heavier". At constant speed it shows 80\,\mathrm{kg} again.

7 Solving problems with Newton's laws

Lecture: p. 4–6 · Giancoli §4-7, §4-8

All the remaining examples follow one recipe, which 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction turns into the free-body diagram method.

Problem-solving steps — Newton's second law
  1. Sketch the situation; choose one body.
  2. Draw every force acting on that body (weight, normal force, rope forces, pushes), and none that it exerts on others.
  3. Choose axes; one along the expected acceleration is convenient.
  4. Split every force into components (F\cos\varphi, F\sin\varphi, signs from the axes).
  5. Write \sum F_x = m a_x, \sum F_y = m a_y (static: = 0).
  6. Solve for the unknowns; check units and limiting cases. With several bodies, repeat for each and link them by the reaction principle and the rope.

Test yourself: a hockey puck slides to the right on frictionless ice. Which free-body diagram is right? Answer: (b). Only gravity and the normal force act on it; nothing pushes it along. "Motion" is not a force, and keeping a velocity needs no force (axiom 1). (Giancoli Fig. 4-20)

Example: street light on two ropes

"Street light with mass m_1 = 20\ \mathrm{kg} hanging from two ropes, which form an angle of \varphi = 20^\circ with the horizontal."

Textbook figure: the light hangs at the lowest point; both ropes rise at 20^\circ to the horizontal. Added on the board: the rope force \vec F_2' at the light and \vec F_2'' at the far end of the right rope.

a) Tension forces pulling on each rope. b) In winter, ropes get a bit shorter ⇒ less sagging. Are the forces acting on the rope smaller or larger? c) Is it possible to pull the rope such that there is no sagging angle, i.e. (… mathematically)?

A massless, taut rope pulls with the same size of force at both ends, inwards along itself: at the light up-right (\vec F_2'), at the pole down-left (\vec F_2''). That is why "the tension in the rope" is one number. "Sagging" is the dip of the ropes; less sag means a smaller angle \varphi.

The light hangs still, so (board) "stationary: \sum \vec F_i = \vec 0", \vec F_1 + \vec F_2 + \vec F_3 = \vec 0, with the three forces on the light: two ropes and the weight.

Board sketch: axes x (right), y (up); at the light, the rope forces \vec F_1 (up-left) and \vec F_2 (up-right), each at \varphi to the horizontal, and the weight \vec F_g downwards.

\vec F_g = 20\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2} \approx 196\ \mathrm N
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} -F_1\cos\varphi \\ F_1\sin\varphi \end{pmatrix}}_{\vec F_1} + \begin{pmatrix} F_2\cos\varphi \\ F_2\sin\varphi \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -mg \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • F_1, F_2 — sizes of the forces with which the left and right rope pull on the light (N)
  • \varphi — angle of each rope with the horizontal (20^\circ)
  • mg — weight of the light (N), the third force \vec F_3 = \vec F_g

Each rope force is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the angle \varphi at the horizontal: horizontal part F\cos\varphi, vertical part F\sin\varphi. The left rope pulls to the left, hence -F_1\cos\varphi; both ropes pull up; the weight pulls straight down.

x: \quad -F_1\cos\varphi + F_2\cos\varphi = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_1 = F_2 = F (the board crosses out \cos\varphi \neq 0). By symmetry the two ropes pull equally hard.

y: insert F_1 = F_2 = F and collect:

F\cdot\sin\varphi + F\cdot\sin\varphi - mg = 0, \qquad F\cdot(2\sin\varphi) = m\cdot g
F = \frac{mg}{2\sin\varphi} = \frac{20\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}}{2\cdot\sin 20^\circ} \approx 287\ \mathrm N
Symbols
  • F — the common rope force (N); other symbols as above

With \sin 20^\circ \approx 0.342: F = 196.2\,\mathrm N / 0.684 \approx 287\,\mathrm N. Answer to a): each rope pulls with about 287\,\mathrm N, more than the light's whole weight (196\,\mathrm N), because most of each rope's force goes sideways and cancels against the other rope.

b) F = \dfrac{m\cdot g}{2\sin\varphi}: "if \varphi decreases, also \sin\varphi decreases." The conclusion the board stops short of: \sin\varphi is in the denominator, so a smaller \sin\varphi makes F larger. In winter the rope forces get larger. With the same light: \varphi = 10^\circ gives F \approx 565\,\mathrm N, \varphi = 5^\circ gives F \approx 1126\,\mathrm N, roughly double each time the angle halves (for small angles \sin\varphi \approx \varphi in rad).

c) \sin\varphi = \dfrac{m\cdot g}{2F}. For \varphi = 0: \dfrac{m\cdot g}{2F} = 0 → "F needs to go to infinity". Solve a) for \sin\varphi; "no sagging" means \sin\varphi = 0, but the numerator mg = 196\,\mathrm N is fixed and non-zero, so the fraction only approaches 0 when F grows without bound. Answer to c): no; a perfectly straight rope with a load in the middle would need an infinite force. That's why power lines sag.

Intuition — why flat ropes need huge forces

Only the vertical parts of the rope forces can hold the light up, and together they must make mg. A steep rope puts most of its force into the vertical; a flat rope puts almost all of it sideways, where the left and right parts just cancel. The flatter the ropes, the larger the total force must be for the small vertical parts to still add up to mg.

Common mistake — \sin or \cos?

Whether the vertical part is F\sin\varphi or F\cos\varphi depends on where the angle is measured. Here \varphi is measured from the horizontal, so the vertical part is F\sin\varphi. If a problem gives the angle to the vertical, it becomes F\cos\varphi. Check with an extreme case: a vertical rope (\varphi = 90^\circ from the horizontal) carries its full force vertically, \sin 90^\circ = 1 ✓.

Pulley blocks

\sum F_i = m\cdot\vec a, \qquad \text{for holding } a = 0

Textbook figure: a worker on a roof lifts a load with a rope over a movable pulley. Two rope segments, each with the tension F_Z, hold the pulley with the load; the worker pulls with F_Z; m\vec g points down. Added on the board: \vec F_Z' at the hook.

Draw a box around "movable pulley + load" and cut the rope where it enters. It cuts through two rope segments, each pulling up with the rope tension F_Z; the only other force is the weight mg. An ideal rope (massless, not stretching) over a frictionless pulley only redirects the pull, so the worker's hand, both segments and the hook all feel F_Z. Holding still means a = 0:

2F_Z - mg = m\cdot a \overset{!}{=} 0, \qquad F_Z = \frac{m\cdot g}{2}
Symbols
  • F_Z — tension in the rope (N) (German Zug), the same in both segments and at the worker's hand
  • m — mass of the load together with the movable pulley (kg)
  • \overset{!}{=} — "must equal": the condition for holding the load still

Half the weight: a 50\,\mathrm{kg} load needs only 245\,\mathrm N.

Intuition — the price

To lift the load by 1 m, both segments must shorten by 1 m, so the worker pulls in 2 m of rope. Half the force over twice the distance: the same work (10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy).

Example: two strings on one mass

Board sketch (p. 6): a mass m hangs from the ceiling on an upper string; a lower string hangs from the mass and is pulled down with the force F; small arrows point to the upper and the lower string. Right: the forces on the mass: F_R up, m\cdot g and F_P down.

The question behind the sketch (not written on the board): two equal strings, you pull on the lower one; which string breaks first? Body: the mass. Forces on it: the upper string up (F_R), gravity down (mg), the lower string down with your pull (F_P). "In order to be static", with up positive:

F_R - mg - F_P = 0, \qquad F_R = F_P + mg > F_P
Symbols
  • F_R — force of the upper string on the mass (N), up
  • F_P — force of the lower string on the mass (N), down: the pull F passed on through the lower string
  • mg — weight of the mass (N)

Since mg > 0, the upper string always carries more. Answer: pulling slowly, the upper string breaks first.

Intuition — and if you jerk?

This is the classic inertia demonstration: a sudden jerk tears the lower string. The heavy mass can't accelerate quickly (a = F/m), so in the short moment of the jerk it barely moves, the upper string is hardly stretched further, and the full jerk lands on the lower string. The board's static equation covers the slow case.

Video link on the board: Seafile (lecture video, AAU login).

Connection

The prep course had Newton's laws and the normal force (2 Dynamics › Newton's laws, 2 Dynamics › Some important forces). The recipe of section 7 becomes the free-body diagram method in 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction.
